newsitem.title: USA: Wall St job hopping rivals Clinton cabinet changes.
newsitem.headline: Wall St job hopping rivals Clinton cabinet changes.

text.p: Not to be outdone by Washington, Wall Street financial wizards have recently been engaged in a burst of job hopping that may rival the turnover in the Clinton cabinet.
New York will not be outdone by Washington. Job hopping by Wall Street financial wizards in recent weeks may even rival the turnover in the Clinton cabinet.
With the U.S. bond market staging a late year rally and the Dow Jones Industrial Average scoring record-breaking gains every day, top flight analysts have become a hot commodity.

"When the markets are moving, be it stock or bond, the shifts tend to accelerate. It's like when you're going into the World Series -- you want to have the right players," said Michael LaTronica, director of research at Gruntal and Co Inc.
Phil Orlando, chief investment officer of Value Line Asset Management, added: "I've got to believe that the sell side is having another good year on top of a very good year" in 1995.
That means Wall Street firms ought to be flush with two back-to-back years of record profitability, Orlando added.
But some Wall Street job hoppers have already made their moves, although shifts are rather rare near year-end.
"Most people will make their move in February after they collect and bank their bonuses," Orlando said.
"It is unusual for people to move in mid-November unless the acquiring company...was willing to compensate them for the bonus that was being given up."
On the other hand, Orlando said job changers may switch because they are concerned about what is going on at their current shop.

So who is going where? For a start, former chief financial economist Steven Ricchiuto and senior economist Waldo Best have jumped ship from BZW Securities Inc to Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, effective Wednesday.
Also this week, Patrick Dimick, who had been a Treasury analyst at CS First Boston Corp, moved to UBS Securities LLC as vice president and government bond strategist.
A few others are planning moves near term, but did not want details made known yet.

In recent months, Michelle Colley Laughlin went from being chief economist at Sanwa Securities to chief Treasuries strategist at Prudential Securities Inc and Joseph Carson left his chief economist post at Dean Witter to take over as chief fixed income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Earlier in the year, John McAuley was named economist at Zions First National Bank after spending time at R.H. Wrightson & Associates and Chemical Bank. Also, Joseph Liro, who had been at S.G. Warburg, became chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

Others have left Wall Street for personal ventures. Lacy Hunt, former chief economist at HSBC Markets Inc, went to Hoisington Inventment Management Co in Austin, Texas, where he is now a money manager. Taking Hunt's place at HSBC was Ian Shepherdson, who had been chief U.K. economist for HSBC.
Meanwhile, Sam Kahan, former chief economist at Fuji Securities, and Allan Leslie, former chief economist at Zions, are now doing economic consulting.

"I enjoyed my time on Wall Street," said Hunt, who spent 23 years there before becoming executive vice president at Hoisington. "I worked for a great organization and loved it. I went around the world nine times.

"But this is a great firm, and money management has been a great interest of mine for a long time," Hunt said, adding that he is happy being back in Texas, where in 1969, he started as a financial economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.

As for the changing of the guard in Washington, resignations started pouring in after Clinton won re-election to a second term in the White House. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, Defense Secretary William Perry, Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary, Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor and White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta are among those leaving. Only Panetta has been replaced.

Near and dear to Wall Street's heart is the question of whether or not market pro and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will stay put. There has been no official announcement yet, but Rubin is expected to continue to safeguard the value of the dollar for another term.

"Rubin has done an outstanding job in tackling some of the issues," said Dimitri Balatsos, president of Tesseract Partners Inc, an investment management firm. "However, there is only so much any administration, any Secretary of the Treasury, any central bank can (do to) influence the currency with words." -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
